parent: III. Clarifying the Gates of Dhyāna-Pāramitā

zh:
行者善尋名故，自知其體。若欲進修，必因門而入。今略明禪門，即為三意：第一、標禪門；第二、解釋；三、料簡。第一、標禪門者，若尋經論所說禪門，乃有無量，原其根本，不過有二，所謂：一、色；二、心。如《摩訶衍》中偈說：
一切諸法中，但有名與色，
若欲如實觀，亦當觀名色。
雖癡心多想，分別於諸法，
更無有一法，出於名色者。
en: The practitioner who has skillfully traced the name thereby comes to know its essence. But to actually advance in cultivation, one must enter through a gate. Here, then, the gates of dhyāna are briefly clarified, under three headings: first, stating the gates; second, explaining them; third, resolving points of doubt.

First, stating the gates: if one traces the gates of dhyāna spoken of throughout the sūtras and treatises, they are limitless in number — but tracing them to their root, they do not exceed two: namely, form, and mind. As the Mahāyāna treatise says in verse:
"Among all dharmas whatsoever, there is only name and form;
If one wishes to observe reality as it truly is, one should likewise observe name and form.
Though a confused mind conceives many notions, discriminating among the various dharmas,
There is not a single dharma that goes beyond name and form."

zh: 今就色門中，即開為二，如經中說：「二為甘露門：一者、不淨觀門；二者、阿那波那門。」心門唯有一門，如經中說：「能觀心性，名為上定。」開色別立於心，此則禪門有三，所謂：一、世間禪門；二、出世間禪門；三、出世間上上禪門。故《大集經》云：「有三種攝心：一者、出法攝心；二者、滅法攝心；三者、非出非滅法攝心。」
en: Now, within the gate of form, this opens further into two, as the sūtra says: "There are two gates to the deathless: first, the gate of the contemplation of impurity; second, the gate of mindfulness of the breath." The gate of mind is a single gate alone, as the sūtra says: "The ability to contemplate the nature of mind is called the supreme concentration." Opening form apart and establishing mind separately, the gates of dhyāna thus number three: namely, the gate of worldly dhyāna; the gate of world-transcending dhyāna; and the gate of dhyāna transcending the world and beyond. Hence the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says: "There are three kinds of gathering the mind: first, gathering the mind through the dharma of emergence; second, gathering the mind through the dharma of extinction; third, gathering the mind through the dharma that is neither emergence nor extinction."

"Name and form" (名色, nāmarūpa) is a term from dependent origination, but Zhiyi uses it here in a wider sense — as shorthand for everything that isn't purely physical (name, i.e. mind) and everything that is (form) — to argue that all of practice reduces to working with mind and body. From there the three gates fall out almost mechanically: form splits into the breath and the body's own impurity; mind stands alone; three gates, three grades of practitioner.

parent: III. Clarifying the Gates of Dhyāna-Pāramitā

zh: 第二、解釋。此三門中，即各為二意：一、別；二、通。第一、別明門者，門名能通，如世門通人，有所至處。一、以息為禪門者，若因息攝心，則能通行心至四禪、四空、四無量心、十六特勝、通明等禪，即是世間禪門，亦名出法攝心。此一往據凡夫禪門。
en: Second, explaining them. Within these three gates, each in turn has two aspects: taken separately, and taken together. First, explaining the gates separately: "gate" means what allows passage through, just as a worldly gate allows a person passage through to wherever they are going.

First, taking the breath as the gate of dhyāna: if the mind is gathered by means of the breath, it can pass through to the four dhyānas, the four formless absorptions, the four immeasurable minds, the sixteen special excellences, the thorough-and-bright concentrations, and the like — this is the gate of worldly dhyāna, also called "gathering the mind through the dharma of emergence." This, broadly speaking, belongs to the dhyāna-gate of ordinary people.

zh: 二、以色為禪門者，如因不淨觀等攝心，則能通行心至九想、八念、十想、背捨、勝處、一切處、次第定、師子奮迅、超越三昧等處，即是出世間禪門，亦名滅法攝心。一往據二乘禪門。三、以心為禪門者，若用智慧反觀心性，則能通行心至法華、念佛、般舟、覺意、首楞嚴諸大三昧及自性禪，乃至清淨淨禪等，是出世間上上禪門，亦名非出非滅法攝心。此一往據菩薩禪門。以此義故，約三法為門。
en: Second, taking form as the gate of dhyāna: if the mind is gathered through the contemplation of impurity and the like, it can pass through to the nine contemplations, the eight recollections, the ten contemplations, the liberations, the stations of mastery, the totality-bases, the sequential concentrations, the lion's-sport samādhi, the transcendence samādhi, and the like — this is the gate of world-transcending dhyāna, also called "gathering the mind through the dharma of extinction." This, broadly speaking, belongs to the dhyāna-gate of the two lesser vehicles.

Third, taking mind as the gate of dhyāna: if wisdom is used to turn contemplation back upon the nature of mind itself, it can pass through to the great samādhis of the Lotus, of buddha-recollection, of pratyutpanna, of awareness, of Śūraṅgama, and the like, together with the dhyāna of self-nature, up through the pure-and-undefiled dhyāna — this is the gate of dhyāna transcending the world and beyond, also called "gathering the mind through the dharma that is neither emergence nor extinction." This, broadly speaking, belongs to the dhyāna-gate of the bodhisattva. It is for this reason that these three things are taken as the gates.

The three gates map onto the three kinds of practitioner named back in topic 1: breath-practice for the ordinary person, contemplation of form for the two lesser vehicles, direct contemplation of mind itself for the bodhisattva. But — as the very next passage insists — this mapping is only "broadly speaking" (一往); Zhiyi immediately goes on to complicate it.

parent: III. Clarifying the Gates of Dhyāna-Pāramitā

zh: 問曰：諸法無量，何故但取此三為禪門？答曰：今略明有三意，故立三法為門：一、如法相；二、隨便易；三、攝法盡。一、如法相者，如《大集經》說：歌羅邏時，即有三事：一、命；二、暖；三、識。出入息者，名為壽命。不臭不爛，名之為暖，即是業持火大故，地、水等色不臭爛也。此中心、意名之為識，即是剎那覺知心也。三法和合，從生至長，無增無減，愚夫不了，於中妄計我、人、眾生，作諸業行，心生染著，顛倒因緣往來三界。若尋其源本，不出此之三法，故以三法為門，不多不少。
en: Question: The dharmas are limitless in number — why take only these three as the gates of dhyāna? Answer: Here, in brief, there are three reasons why these three things are established as gates: first, because they match the very mark of what a living being is; second, because they are convenient and easy to follow; third, because they encompass every dharma completely.

First, because they match the very mark of what a living being is: as the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says, at the stage of the kalala — the earliest embryonic stage — three things are already present: life, warmth, and consciousness. The breath, going out and coming in, is called "life." Not decaying and not putrefying is called "warmth" — this is because karma sustains the fire element, so that the earth, water, and other elements of form do not decay or putrefy. Mind and intention here are called "consciousness" — that is, the mind that is aware moment by moment. These three things, joined together, carry a being from birth through growth, neither increasing nor decreasing — yet the foolish and unenlightened, failing to understand this, wrongly conceive of a self, a person, and sentient beings within it, carry out every kind of karmic action, give rise to a defiled and attached mind, and, through inverted causes and conditions, come and go through the three realms. If one traces this to its very source, it never goes beyond these three things — hence these three are taken as the gates, neither more nor fewer.

zh: 二、隨便易故，立三法為門者，如因息修禪，則有二便：一、疾得禪定；二、易悟無常。以色為門，亦有二便：一、能斷貪欲；二、易了虛假。心為門者，此亦有二便：一、能降一切煩惱；二、易悟空理。三、攝法盡者，此三法是禪門根本故。所以者何？舉要說三，開即無量。如息門中，或數或隨，或時觀息，如此非一，至處亦異。如色門中，或緣外色，或緣內色，或作慈悲，或緣佛相，乃至得解實觀，如此非一，至處亦異。如心門中，或止或觀，或覺或了，或覺了諸心入於非心，覺了非心出無量心，或覺了非心非不心，能知一切心非心，如是緣心不同，至處亦復非一，故說三門攝一切禪門。此事至第七、八釋修證中方乃可見。
en: Second, because they are convenient and easy to follow, these three things are established as gates: cultivating dhyāna by means of the breath brings two conveniences — first, concentration is quickly attained; second, impermanence is easily realized. Taking form as the gate likewise brings two conveniences — first, craving and desire can be severed; second, what is illusory and unreal is easily understood. Taking mind as the gate likewise brings two conveniences — first, every affliction can be subdued; second, the principle of emptiness is easily realized.

Third, because they encompass every dharma completely: these three things are the root of every gate of dhyāna. Why is this? Taking the essentials, only three are named — but opened out, they are limitless. Within the gate of the breath, there is counting, following, and at times observing the breath directly — these are not one single thing, and where they lead also differs. Within the gate of form, there is taking an external form as the object, taking an internal form as the object, cultivating loving-kindness and compassion, taking the Buddha's marks as the object, and further, attaining understanding through the contemplation of reality — these too are not one single thing, and where they lead also differs. Within the gate of mind, there is śamatha and vipaśyanā, awareness and clear knowing, becoming clearly aware that every mind enters into "not-mind," becoming clearly aware that "not-mind" gives rise to measureless minds, or becoming clearly aware that it is neither "not-mind" nor "not not-mind," able to know that every mind is not a fixed mind — taking the mind as object in these various ways, where they lead is likewise not one single thing. Hence it is said that these three gates encompass every gate of dhyāna whatsoever. This matter will only become fully visible further below, in the seventh and eighth topics, where cultivation and realization are explained.

The first justification is the most striking: Zhiyi grounds the three gates not in scripture or tradition but in a claim about what a living being actually is, down to the earliest moment of conception — the kalala stage, where life (breath), warmth (the fire element sustaining the body), and consciousness are already present together. The three gates of practice, in other words, simply work with the same three things that constitute a living being in the first place.

parent: III. Clarifying the Gates of Dhyāna-Pāramitā

zh: 第二、通名三門者，此三法通得作世間、出世間、出世間上上等禪門。所以者何？一、如息法不定，但屬世間禪門。何以得知？如《毘尼》中，佛為聲聞弟子說觀息等十六行法，弟子隨教而修，皆得聖道，故知亦是出世間禪門，即大乘門者，如《大品》說：「阿那波那，即是菩薩摩訶衍。」故《請觀音經》約數息辨六字章句，明三乘得道，此豈可但是世間禪門？
en: Second, explaining the three gates taken together: these three things can, in fact, each serve as the gate of worldly dhyāna, world-transcending dhyāna, or dhyāna transcending the world and beyond alike. Why is this?

First, the method of the breath is not fixed to belonging only to the gate of worldly dhyāna. How can this be known? As in the Vinaya, where the Buddha teaches his śrāvaka disciples the sixteen practices of observing the breath, and the disciples, cultivating in accordance with this teaching, all attain the noble path — hence it can be known that this is also the gate of world-transcending dhyāna. That it is also the Mahāyāna gate can be seen from the Larger Sūtra, which says: "Mindfulness of the breath is itself the bodhisattva's Mahāyāna." Hence the Sūtra of Invoking Avalokiteśvara explains the six-syllable formula in terms of counting the breath, clarifying how all three vehicles attain the path through it — how, then, could this be merely the gate of worldly dhyāna?

zh: 二、色法為門，亦不得但是二乘所行，不通大乘及凡夫、外道。何以故？如《涅槃》中說：「外道但能治色，不能治心，我弟子善治於心。」故知凡夫亦得觀色。大乘觀色，如《大品》中說：「脹想、爛想等，是菩薩摩訶衍。」此豈可但是出世間禪門？三、約心為門，亦不得但據菩薩。何以故？如外道亦觀心起四十八見，凡夫緣心入四空，通聲聞者，如《涅槃》說：「我弟子善治心故，能離三界。」此豈唯是出世間上上禪門？當知三門互通，但三種人用心異故，發禪得道亦各不同。此義至第九、明從禪波羅蜜起教中，當廣分別。
en: Second, taking form as the gate cannot be said to belong only to the practice of the two lesser vehicles, without extending to the Mahāyāna, or to ordinary people and non-Buddhist practitioners. Why is this? As the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says: "Non-Buddhist practitioners can only treat form, and cannot treat mind; my own disciples treat mind well." Hence it can be known that ordinary people, too, can contemplate form. That the Mahāyāna also contemplates form can be seen from the Larger Sūtra, which says: "The contemplation of swelling, the contemplation of putrefaction, and the like are themselves the bodhisattva's Mahāyāna." How, then, could this be merely the gate of world-transcending dhyāna?

Third, taking mind as the gate cannot be said to belong only to bodhisattvas. Why is this? Non-Buddhist practitioners, too, contemplate mind and give rise to the forty-eight wrong views from it; ordinary people take mind as the object and enter the four formless absorptions; and as for its extending to the śrāvakas, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says: "Because my disciples treat mind well, they are able to leave the three realms behind." How, then, could this be only the gate of dhyāna transcending the world and beyond? One should know that these three gates interpenetrate one another — it is only that, because the three kinds of practitioners use the mind differently, the dhyāna they give rise to, and the path they attain, likewise each differ. This point will be explained fully further below, in the ninth topic, where the teachings arising from dhyāna-pāramitā are clarified.

Having just mapped each gate to one kind of practitioner, Zhiyi now takes the mapping apart again — with scriptural counter-examples for every case: śrāvakas reaching the noble path through breath-practice, ordinary people and even non-Buddhist practitioners contemplating form, non-Buddhists and śrāvakas alike working with mind. The lesson is not that the earlier three-way mapping was wrong, but that it was only ever a rough default ("broadly speaking," as the previous section put it) — any gate can, in principle, be walked by any practitioner, and what actually differs between them is how the mind is used once inside the gate, not which gate is entered.

quiz.q: The gates of dhyāna are limitless, but traced to their root they "do not exceed two." Which two?
options: form and mind
contaminated and uncontaminated
śamatha and vipaśyanā
precepts and concentration
quiz.why: "If one traces the gates of dhyāna spoken of throughout the sūtras and treatises, they are limitless in number — but tracing them to their root, they do not exceed two: namely, form, and mind." The verse on name and form is cited as support.

quiz.q: The gate of form opens into two. Which are the "two gates to the deathless" the sūtra names?
options: the contemplation of impurity and mindfulness of the breath
loving-kindness and dependent origination
buddha-recollection and analysis of elements
counting the breath and contemplating mind
quiz.why: "Within the gate of form, this opens further into two, as the sūtra says: 'There are two gates to the deathless: first, the gate of the contemplation of impurity; second, the gate of mindfulness of the breath.'" The breath is form, so it falls under the gate of form; the gate of mind is single.

quiz.q: The gate of mind is a single gate. What sūtra line does the text cite?
options: dhyāna held in a bodhisattva's mind is called pāramitā
mindfulness of the breath is the bodhisattva's Mahāyāna
the ability to contemplate the nature of mind is called the supreme concentration
deeply cultivating dhyāna, one attains the five powers
quiz.why: "The gate of mind is a single gate alone, as the sūtra says: 'The ability to contemplate the nature of mind is called the supreme concentration.'" The other three are quotations from elsewhere in the fascicle, about the powers, the breath as Mahāyāna, and the unshared name.

quiz.q: Of the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra's three ways of gathering the mind, which gate corresponds to "gathering the mind through the dharma that is neither emergence nor extinction"?
options: the gate of form, world-transcending dhyāna
the gate of the breath, worldly dhyāna
none of the three gates
the gate of mind, dhyāna transcending the world and beyond
quiz.why: The breath is "the gate of worldly dhyāna, also called gathering the mind through the dharma of emergence"; form is world-transcending dhyāna, the dharma of extinction; mind is "the gate of dhyāna transcending the world and beyond, also called gathering the mind through the dharma that is neither emergence nor extinction."

quiz.q: How does the text explain the word "gate"?
options: a gate is a lineage of teachers
"gate" means what allows passage, just as a worldly gate lets a person through to where they are going
a gate shuts, keeping evil out
a gate is a chapter of scripture
quiz.why: "'Gate' means what allows passage through, just as a worldly gate allows a person passage through to wherever they are going." Closing the six faculties against evil is about precepts in the first topic, not the meaning of "gate."

quiz.q: Taking the breath as the gate, which dhyānas does the text say it leads to?
options: the nine contemplations, eight recollections, ten contemplations, liberations, stations of mastery
the four dhyānas, four formless absorptions, four immeasurable minds, sixteen special excellences, thorough-and-bright concentrations
the Lotus, buddha-recollection, pratyutpanna, Śūraṅgama
the samādhi of self-nature up through the pure-and-undefiled
quiz.why: "If the mind is gathered by means of the breath, it can pass through to the four dhyānas, the four formless absorptions, the four immeasurable minds, the sixteen special excellences, the thorough-and-bright concentrations, and the like — this is the gate of worldly dhyāna." The nine contemplations and liberations come through the gate of form; the Lotus, Śūraṅgama, and samādhi of self-nature through the gate of mind.

quiz.q: Taking mind as the gate, what is the method, and to whom does it broadly belong?
options: gathering the mind by impurity; broadly the two vehicles' gate
reciting mantras; broadly non-Buddhists
gathering the mind by the breath; broadly the ordinary person's gate
using wisdom to turn contemplation back on the nature of mind; broadly the bodhisattva's gate
quiz.why: "Taking mind as the gate of dhyāna: if wisdom is used to turn contemplation back upon the nature of mind itself, it can pass through to the great samādhis ... This, broadly speaking, belongs to the dhyāna-gate of the bodhisattva." The breath broadly belongs to ordinary people and form to the two vehicles.

quiz.q: Taking form as the gate, such as the contemplation of impurity, which dhyānas does it lead to, and which gate is it?
options: the Lotus, pratyutpanna, Śūraṅgama; dhyāna beyond the world
the four dhyānas, formless absorptions, immeasurables; worldly dhyāna
the six wondrous gates, sixteen excellences, thorough-and-bright; both
the nine contemplations through the transcendence samādhi; the gate of world-transcending dhyāna
quiz.why: "If the mind is gathered through the contemplation of impurity and the like, it can pass through to the nine contemplations, the eight recollections, the ten contemplations, the liberations, the stations of mastery, the totality-bases, the sequential concentrations, the lion's-sport samādhi, the transcendence samādhi, and the like — this is the gate of world-transcending dhyāna."

quiz.q: Why only these three as gates? Which three reasons does the text give?
options: matching the mark of what a living being is; convenient and easy; encompassing every dharma
taught by the Buddha, transmitted by patriarchs, given by teachers
counting, following, stilling
worldly, world-transcending, beyond the world
quiz.why: "There are three reasons why these three things are established as gates: first, because they match the very mark of what a living being is; second, because they are convenient and easy to follow; third, because they encompass every dharma completely." Worldly and the rest are the gates' names, not the reasons; counting, following, and stilling are the first three wondrous gates.

quiz.q: Under "matching the mark," the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says three things are present at the kalala stage. Which pairing is correct?
options: the breath is consciousness; not decaying is life; mind is warmth
the breath is warmth; not decaying is consciousness; mind is life
the breath is life; not decaying is warmth; mind and intention are consciousness
the three are earth, water, and fire
quiz.why: "The breath, going out and coming in, is called 'life.' Not decaying and not putrefying is called 'warmth' — this is because karma sustains the fire element ... Mind and intention here are called 'consciousness.'" Life matches the breath gate, warmth (the body) the form gate, consciousness the mind gate — hence three, neither more nor fewer.

quiz.q: Under "convenient and easy," what two conveniences does the gate of mind bring?
options: craving can be severed; the illusory is easily understood
concentration is quickly attained; impermanence is easily realized
every affliction can be subdued; the principle of emptiness is easily realized
powers are gained; heavenly rebirth comes easily
quiz.why: "Taking mind as the gate likewise brings two conveniences — first, every affliction can be subdued; second, the principle of emptiness is easily realized." The breath brings swift concentration and insight into impermanence; form brings severing craving and understanding the illusory.

quiz.q: Under "encompassing every dharma," how does the text show the three gates include every gate of dhyāna?
options: every gate outside the three is non-Buddhist
the three gates are three sitting postures
a fourth gate is needed to include everything
only three are named in essentials, but opened out they are limitless — the breath gate alone has counting, following, observing, each leading somewhere different
quiz.why: "These three things are the root of every gate of dhyāna. Why is this? Taking the essentials, only three are named — but opened out, they are limitless. Within the gate of the breath, there is counting, following, and at times observing the breath directly — these are not one single thing, and where they lead also differs."

quiz.q: How does the text show that the breath is not merely a worldly gate but also a world-transcending one?
options: because counting the breath cures illness
because non-Buddhists also count the breath
because counting the breath yields the four dhyānas
in the Vinaya the Buddha taught śrāvakas the sixteen practices of observing the breath, and they all attained the noble path
quiz.why: "As in the Vinaya, where the Buddha teaches his śrāvaka disciples the sixteen practices of observing the breath, and the disciples, cultivating in accordance with this teaching, all attain the noble path — hence it can be known that this is also the gate of world-transcending dhyāna." Attaining the four dhyānas alone would still be worldly.

quiz.q: Which line from the Nirvāṇa Sūtra does the text cite to show ordinary people and non-Buddhists can contemplate form?
options: non-Buddhists can only treat form, not mind; my disciples treat mind well
buddha-nature has five names
the contemplations of swelling and putrefaction are the bodhisattva's Mahāyāna
because my disciples treat mind well, they leave the three realms
quiz.why: "As the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says: 'Non-Buddhist practitioners can only treat form, and cannot treat mind; my own disciples treat mind well.' Hence it can be known that ordinary people, too, can contemplate form." The line about leaving the three realms shows the mind gate extends to śrāvakas, and swelling and putrefaction come from the Larger Sūtra.

quiz.q: If the three gates interpenetrate, why do the three kinds of practitioners attain different dhyānas and paths?
options: they have different teachers
they practice for different lengths of time
the three kinds of practitioners use the mind differently
they enter different gates
quiz.why: "One should know that these three gates interpenetrate one another — it is only that, because the three kinds of practitioners use the mind differently, the dhyāna they give rise to, and the path they attain, likewise each differ." The difference is in how the mind is used, not which gate is entered.
